note: Raw verified corpus for ground.json. Every finding here was researched by fetching its source, then independently re-checked by a second pass that fetched the same URL and could reject or reword the claim. 66 of 66 survived; 24 were reworded to be weaker and more honest than first written. method: artbitrage ground-truth workflow, 72 agents: 6 topic researchers, 66 adversarial verifiers (one per claim, each instructed to default to rejection when uncertain).

findings.statement: Any UK building built or refurbished before 2000 may contain asbestos. HSE's list of asbestos-containing materials found in homes includes cement products (pipes, flues, roofs), pipe and boiler lagging, textured decorative coatings (Artex), floor tiles, asbestos insulating board and more — asbestos was widely used in homes until it was banned in 1999.
findings.detail: HSE's own list of asbestos-containing materials found in homes: 'asbestos cement products (pipes, flues, roofs etc), lagging (on pipes and boilers etc), water tanks and toilet cisterns, asbestos insulating board (AIB), loose asbestos in ceiling and wall cavities, sprayed coatings, textured decorative coatings (commonly referred to as Artex), floor tiles, textiles and composites'. So construction rubble buried in a garden of a pre-2000 house — old garage roof, shed panels, offcuts, tiles — should be treated as potentially asbestos-containing until shown otherwise. Buried asbestos cement typically shows up as hard, grey, brittle cement fragments, often with the corrugated profile of old garage/shed roofs.

source.name: HSE — Asbestos FAQs

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot establish that any particular grey fragment in this garden IS asbestos — visual identification is unreliable; only lab analysis of a sample (about £10-£40 at UKAS labs, a cost I did not verify) confirms it. The visual description of buried fragments is my summary, not a quote from HSE.

findings.statement: Asbestos only harms you when fibres get into the air and are breathed in; material that is intact and undisturbed is normally left in place, not ripped out.
findings.detail: HSE: asbestos 'only becomes a risk to human health when it is released into the air and breathed in', and 'where asbestos containing materials are assessed as being in good condition and not in a position where they are likely to be damaged they should be left in place and monitored'. For a digger this means: a whole, wet, muddy piece of cement sheet lifted gently is a low-fibre-release event; snapping, crushing under boots, or dry-sweeping fragments is exactly what creates the airborne dust that matters. The harm is also cumulative and slow (asbestos diseases take decades) — one careful encounter is not an emergency, so there is no reason to rush.

source.name: HSE — Asbestos FAQs

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot establish that any single brief exposure is zero-risk — HSE's position is that risk scales with fibre dose, not that low doses are proven safe. Also cannot quantify how many fibres a given act of breakage releases.

findings.statement:
HSE equipment sheet em5 (Wetting asbestos materials) says it in as many words: "Damp asbestos materials release far fewer asbestos fibres into the air", and "Wet the asbestos materials before starting any work. Don't work on dry asbestos materials." On method: "Water on its own does not effectively wet asbestos-containing materials, wetting agents should be used" — diluted per the maker's instructions, usually 10–15 parts water to 1 part wetting agent, or 8 parts water to 1 part liquid detergent as an alternative. Let the spray "fall" onto the material rather than hit it as a jet, spray at low pressure with a slow backwards-and-forwards motion, and don't over-wet: "Over-wetting material can create a waste slurry which will be difficult to clean up."

What em5 does not mention is soil, burial or spoil heaps. It is written for trained people working on asbestos materials in buildings, and it opens by saying you must be trained to do that work at all. So the digging inference is ours, not HSE's: if damp releases far fewer fibres than dry, then fragments lying in damp subsoil should be releasing less than the same fragments after they have dried out in sun and wind and are then trodden on or swept. That follows from the same physics, but two limits are worth keeping in view — "far fewer fibres" is not "safe", a word HSE never uses here, and em5 warns that some asbestos materials "cannot be wetted all the way through", so a damp surface is no proof of a damp core.
findings.detail: HSE equipment sheet em5 states it plainly: 'Damp asbestos materials release far fewer asbestos fibres into the air' and 'Don't work on dry asbestos materials.' Method: spray with water plus a little washing-up liquid (about 8 parts water to 1 part detergent — plain water alone doesn't wet asbestos well), let the spray fall gently onto the material rather than jetting it, and don't drench it into a slurry. Practical upshot for someone digging now: material sitting in damp subsoil is in its least hazardous state; the risk rises after you dig it up, when fragments dry in sun and wind and then get stepped on or swept.

source.name: HSE Asbestos Essentials sheet em5 — Wetting asbestos materials

findings.cannot_establish: em5 is written for trained non-licensed workers, not homeowners; it does not give a number for how much wetting reduces fibre release, and dampness does not make handling licensed materials (lagging, insulating board) acceptable for a householder.

findings.statement: On finding suspected asbestos while digging, HSE small-works guidance (sheet a14) and council householder guidance point the same way: stop, keep people away, keep the material damp, avoid breaking it and take care not to crush debris underfoot, and either leave it in place or double-wrap whole pieces in heavy (1000-gauge) polythene sealed with tape; clean up only with damp rags, and on no account use a domestic vacuum cleaner. (Neither document is written for the dig-discovery moment itself — this combines their handling rules; if in doubt, phone the council's environmental services before touching anything.)
findings.detail: This is HSE sheet a14 plus council householder guidance combined. HSE a14: 'Avoid or minimise breaking the AC', caution 'There may be AC debris on the ground. Be careful not to crush this', double-wrap large pieces in 1000-gauge polythene sealed with duct tape, clean the area with damp rags, wear disposable overalls and respiratory protection. Lancaster City Council to householders: 'Thoroughly wet the waste with clean water before handling', 'Avoid breaking the asbestos waste', keep others away, wash well afterwards, bag used overalls/masks as asbestos waste, and 'ON NO ACCOUNT SHOULD A DOMESTIC VACUUM CLEANER BE USED'. If in any doubt, phone the council's environmental health team before touching anything — that call is free.

source.name: Lancaster City Council — Disposal of asbestos waste from the home (with HSE sheet a14, hse.gov.uk/pubns/guidance/a14.Pdf, also fetched)

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot establish that a bare-handed, unmasked householder doing this is risk-free — both documents assume PPE including a proper respirator (FFP3-class), and a14 is formally aimed at trained workers. Also cannot establish that leaving fragments buried is lawful in every situation (deliberate burial of asbestos waste is not a disposal route).

findings.statement: Fibrous asbestos — pipe lagging, sprayed coating, insulating board — is far more dangerous than cement sheet and is licensed-contractor work only; a householder should not handle it at all.
findings.detail: Lancaster's householder sheet, in capitals: 'FIBROUS ASBESTOS, SUCH AS PIPE LAGGING SHOULD ONLY BE REMOVED BY A LICENCED SPECIALIST CONTRACTOR... IT IS TOO DANGEROUS FOR THE HOUSEHOLDER TO HANDLE.' HSE a14 draws the same line for tradespeople: the cement-sheet method 'is not appropriate if other asbestos-containing materials are present, eg lagging, limpet or insulating board. Use an HSE-licensed contractor for such work.' Buried lagging looks like crumbly, fibrous, often white/grey/blue-grey plaster-like wrap, sometimes still curved in pipe shapes — soft and fluffy where cement sheet is hard. If what you have unearthed crumbles like old plaster and shows fibres, stop completely, dampen it, cover it, and get professionals.

source.name: Lancaster City Council householder asbestos guidance (with HSE a14)

findings.cannot_establish: The visual description of buried lagging is my plain-words gloss, not quoted from either source. Neither source quantifies how much more fibre lagging releases than cement — 'far more dangerous' is the regulators' categorical judgement (licensed vs non-licensed), not a measured ratio I can cite.

findings.statement: Many UK councils — but not all — give householders a legal, low-cost route for small amounts of bonded asbestos: free drop-off of double-wrapped sheets or bags at a designated household waste site, or a paid collection. The rules are strictly council-specific (quantity caps, booking, which sites), trade waste is always excluded, and some councils accept none at their sites at all. Lancaster is a real example: its householder guidance (council PDF dated April 2011, still hosted) states a maximum of six double-wrapped sheets OR six bags per month, at most three deliveries a year, wrapping materials supplied free, non-compliant loads refused, and builders' waste directed to a licensed facility; the council's current web page still confirms the drop-off route, free wrapping materials and trade-waste exclusion, though it no longer states those numeric limits. All asbestos waste is classed as hazardous/special waste. So the honest advice to a digger stands: phone your own council's waste team first and ask 'do you take double-wrapped asbestos cement at the tip?' and 'do you run a collection service?' before hiring anyone.
findings.detail: Lancaster's arrangement (a real example, not a national rule): householders may deliver 'a MAXIMUM of six sheets of asbestos, double wrapped in visqueen, OR six bags of asbestos per month' to the household waste recycling centre, maximum three deliveries a year, wrapping materials supplied free; non-compliant loads are refused; builders' waste is not accepted and must go to a licensed facility. All asbestos waste is classed as hazardous/special waste. So the honest advice to a digger is: phone your own council's environmental health or waste team first and ask two questions — 'do you take double-wrapped asbestos cement at the tip?' and 'do you run a collection service?' — before hiring anyone.

source.name: Lancaster City Council householder asbestos guidance

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot establish that YOUR council offers this — provision, quantities and charges vary widely by authority, and this Lancaster document dates from 2011 so even its own prices are stale. Verify locally before loading the car.

findings.statement: Urban and made-ground garden soil commonly contains lead — UKHSA cites past industry, smelters and leaded-petrol deposition near busy roads; chipped old paint is another documented source (Minnesota Dept of Health) — but, per UKHSA, "generally not in concentrations that can affect your normal enjoyment of the garden or growing flowers and vegetables". The risk pathway the guidance addresses is children swallowing soil (most toddlers eat some at some point; pica of ~1-5 g/day warrants a GP visit and possibly a blood lead test), not adult contact, which the page does not discuss.
findings.detail: UKHSA guidance on GOV.UK: 'Soil in most urban areas contains chemicals such as lead, but generally not in concentrations that can affect your normal enjoyment of the garden.' The concern it flags is children: most toddlers eat some soil sometime, and a child with pica (recurrent eating of soil, of the order of 1-5 g/day) should be discussed with a GP, who may recommend a blood lead test; UKHSA and the council can then check historic land use and arrange soil sampling. Recommended controls are behavioural and physical: supervise small children in the garden and lay a barrier (e.g. decking) over bare soil sections. Old paint flakes in dug-up debris are a classic lead source (the Minnesota Health Dept page lists 'chipped paint containing lead' among common soil contaminants) — so don't burn, sand or crush painted fragments, and wash hands before eating.

source.name: GOV.UK / UKHSA — Lead: information for the public

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot establish the lead level in any particular garden without a lab test — 'most urban areas are fine' is a population statement, and gardens next to demolished painted buildings, old orchards, or former works can be well above typical. The paint-flake detail comes from a US source, not the UKHSA page.

findings.statement: How dangerous lead-bearing soil is for growing vegetables is genuinely contested in the UK: the 2014 Category 4 Screening Level for allotment soil is 80 mg/kg lead (for residential land with home-grown produce it is 200 mg/kg), yet a 2019 Newcastle/Northumbria universities study of city allotments whose soils averaged 550 mg/kg found lead in vegetables typically below national food safety guidelines, and blood samples from 43 gardeners versus 28 non-gardening neighbours showed no statistically significant difference. The researchers argue the screening guidance is 'overly cautious' for urban allotments because aged, weathered lead stays tightly bound to soil. So a soil test above 80 mg/kg means 'investigate and take sensible precautions', not 'your garden is poisoned'. (Standard precautions — washing produce, peeling root veg, washing hands, covering bare soil — are widely advised, though they come from general guidance rather than this study's press release.)
findings.detail: The 2014 Category 4 Screening Level used for residential land with home-grown produce is around 80 mg/kg lead. Newcastle University's 2019 study of city allotments found soils averaging 550 mg/kg; lead in parsnips, carrots, leeks and onions 'typically remained below national food safety guidelines'; blood samples from 43 gardeners versus 28 non-gardening neighbours showed no statistically significant difference; and the researchers argue the UK screening guidance is 'overly cautious' because aged, weathered lead binds to soil and is not mobile. So a soil test above 80 mg/kg means 'investigate and take sensible precautions', not 'your garden is poisoned'. The precautions that everyone agrees on: wash produce, peel root veg, wash hands, keep bare soil covered.

source.name: Newcastle University press release — lead in allotment soil study

findings.cannot_establish: This is one study, summarised in the university's own press release (an interested party for its finding), with small blood-sample numbers; it cannot establish that high-lead soil is safe in general, especially for toddlers who eat soil directly rather than washed vegetables. The official 80 mg/kg screening value remains the regulatory reference; I verified it only via this secondary source, not the Environment Agency C4SL document itself.

findings.statement: For growing food in suspect soil, the Minnesota Department of Health says the main exposure route is swallowing soil and soil dust — on hands, and clinging to produce — rather than the plant drawing contaminants up into itself. It acknowledges uptake does happen ("some harmful contaminants are taken into and may build up in produce"), but "the levels found in produce are lower than levels found in soil". Its practical list, which a UK gardener can borrow even though the guidance is written for Minnesota: use raised beds with clean soil; thoroughly wash all produce; discard the outer leaves of leafy vegetables; peel or thoroughly scrub root vegetables; cover bare soil with untreated wood chips or plants; wash hands well after gardening; and watch that children don't get soil or dust from hands and toys into their mouths. MDH also notes that testing "may not always be necessary" — you can follow these steps instead. It frames all of this as lowering risk, not removing it, and does not say how much. That caution is earned: UK studies of heavily contaminated allotments have found estimated lead intakes well above tolerable limits despite washing, because soil clinging to produce is hard to remove completely. So the steps shift the odds considerably; on genuinely contaminated ground they are not a substitute for finding out what is in the soil.
findings.detail: Minnesota Department of Health (US state health agency): 'the greatest risk of exposure to contaminants... is from contaminated soil getting into your mouth or by breathing in contaminated dust', and contaminant levels 'found in produce are lower than levels found in soil'. Its practical list transfers directly to a UK garden: use raised beds filled with soil from a clean source; thoroughly wash all produce; discard outer leaves of leafy veg; peel or scrub root vegetables (the crops in direct soil contact are the least suitable for suspect ground); cover bare soil with untreated wood chips or planting; wash hands after gardening. Notably it also says testing 'may not always be necessary' — the precautions work whether or not you test.

source.name: Minnesota Department of Health — Gardening in urban soil

findings.cannot_establish: US guidance, not UK — the principles (pathway ranking, hygiene measures) are general, but it carries no UK regulatory weight and does not cover every contaminant (e.g. some organics do enter plants more readily than lead).

findings.statement: Old treated timber dug from a garden — greenish (CCA, contains arsenic) or black/tarry (creosote, a carcinogen) — should never be burned: NPIC says the smoke and ash can be toxic. UK law has, since 30 June 2003 (SI 2003/721, carried forward into UK REACH Annex XVII), banned using creosote-treated wood in parks, gardens and outdoor recreational facilities where there is a risk of frequent skin contact, in garden furniture, in containers intended for growing, and in packaging that may come into contact with food or feed; second-hand sleepers may be re-sold but the same use restrictions apply. CCA's arsenic can leach to the wood's surface and onto skin, and from reused boards into surrounding soil; the US residential phase-out began in 2004, with the EU/UK restricting arsenic-treated wood around the same period.
findings.detail: CCA (chromated copper arsenate) gave timber a green tinge and was phased out of residential use from 2004 (US date; the EU/UK restricted it around the same period): the arsenic 'can leach to the surface and get on the skin', leaches 'into the surrounding soil', and burning it is the worst move — 'the smoke and ash can be toxic'; cutting and sanding without protection creates hazardous dust, and reuse around vegetables is advised against. Creosote: the UK Creosote (Prohibition on Use and Marketing) Regulations 2003 ban treated wood 'in parks, gardens and outdoor recreational and leisure facilities where there is a risk of frequent skin contact', in garden furniture, in containers for growing, and near food — old railway sleepers may be re-sold second-hand but the same use restrictions apply. Practical rule for the digger: old green-tinged or tar-smelling timber goes to the tip as treated-wood waste (ask the council), never on the bonfire, never into a new veg bed.

source.name: NPIC (National Pesticide Information Center, Oregon State University) — CCA FAQ; plus legislation.gov.uk SI 2003/721 (fetched)

findings.cannot_establish: The 2004 CCA phase-out date is the US one (NPIC); I did not verify the exact UK/EU CCA restriction date from a primary source. Green tinge fades with age, so absence of colour does not prove untreated wood. Evidence that CCA beds measurably raise arsenic in vegetables is itself mixed — the ban is precautionary.

findings.statement: Before digging deeper or driving in posts, treat buried pipes and cables as present until located — HSE's HSG47 says plainly, "Underground services are widespread. Assume they are present unless you have been shown otherwise," and sets out three elements of safe work: planning the work, locating and identifying buried services, and safe excavation. It applies "where underground services may be found and disturbed", a list that ends with "any other work that involves penetrating the ground at or below surface level"; it is written for people commissioning and carrying out work, but the method transfers straight to a garden. In practice that is: a detecting device used "in conjunction with up-to-date service plans" (para 80), then careful hand digging near anything indicated — and note that plans "do not normally show the position of gas service connections", so old gardens hide runs to sheds and garages that no plan records. Treat soil cuts seriously too: the NHS says "there is a risk of tetanus if soil or manure containing bacteria gets into a wound", with higher risk if "the wound is very dirty or there is something stuck in the wound". So dig made ground in proper gloves, clean any wound at once, and see a GP or call NHS 111 if dirt stays in it after cleaning, it turns hot or swollen, or you are not sure you are fully vaccinated (the NHS notes the tetanus vaccine "has routinely been given since 1961").
findings.detail: HSG47 (HSE's guidance on underground services) applies to any 'work involving penetrating the ground at or below surface level' and rests on three steps: plan the work, locate and identify buried services (up-to-date service plans plus a detecting device), then dig carefully — hand-digging near where services are indicated. In a domestic garden the gas, water and electricity supply runs typically come in from the street to the meter positions, and old gardens also hide unrecorded runs to sheds and garages. On sharps: rubble layers carry broken glass and rusted metal, and the NHS notes tetanus follows when 'soil or manure containing bacteria gets into a wound', with risk higher when 'the wound is very dirty or there is something stuck in the wound' — so dig made ground in proper gloves, clean any wound immediately, and contact NHS 111 if the wound stays dirty, shows infection, or your vaccination status is uncertain (UK routine tetanus vaccination began in 1961; many adults are covered but not all boosted).

source.name: HSE HSG47 — Avoiding danger from underground services; plus NHS tetanus page (nhs.uk/conditions/tetanus/, fetched)

findings.cannot_establish: HSG47 is written for work/employers, not householders, and no free service tells a homeowner where their own private garden runs are — plans from LSBUD/utilities cover mains, not the unrecorded cable a previous owner ran to the shed. The 'typical service routes' sentence is my inference, not from the fetched pages.

findings.statement: 'Made ground' is the geologist's term for ground people deposited — BGS defines it as 'artificial deposits, such as embankments and spoil heaps, on the natural ground surface'. A separate BGS report on classifying artificial ground (OR/10/036) explains why it matters: previously developed ground 'is often associated with potentially contaminated material, unpredictable engineering conditions and unstable ground'. Councils have a statutory duty under Part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act 1990 to identify contaminated land, and land only meets the legal definition when a source, a pathway and a receptor all connect. Practical upshot: brick rubble and clinker alone are ordinary made ground, not an emergency; paid soil testing earns its cost when suspect material, a real exposure route and someone exposed all line up — and a call to the council's environmental health / contaminated land team is free, since they are the ones who investigate historic land use in your area.
findings.detail: British Geological Survey: artificial ground is 'areas where the ground surface has been significantly modified by human activity'; made ground specifically is 'artificial deposits, such as embankments and spoil heaps, on the natural ground surface' — and previously developed ground 'is often associated with potentially contaminated material, unpredictable engineering conditions and unstable ground'. Councils have a statutory duty (Part 2A, Environmental Protection Act 1990) to identify contaminated land, and use the source-pathway-receptor test: land is only 'contaminated land' when a contaminant, a route, and someone/something exposed all connect. Translation for a homeowner: finding brick rubble and clinker is normal made ground, not an emergency. Testing earns its cost when all three line up — visible suspect material (ash, chemical smells, paint, extensive debris) PLUS a real pathway (children playing on bare soil, food grown in the ground) PLUS a receptor. A phone call to the council's environmental health/contaminated land officer is free, and they hold the historic land-use maps that say what your plot used to be.

source.name: British Geological Survey — artificial ground; plus Harborough District Council contaminated land FAQ (fetched)

findings.cannot_establish: Cannot give a verified price for domestic soil testing (commercial labs quote roughly low hundreds of pounds, but I did not verify this from any fetched source), and cannot establish that a single garden sample is representative — made ground is patchy by nature, which is a real limit on cheap one-sample tests. The 'when testing is worth it' rule is my synthesis of the source-pathway-receptor framework, not a quoted checklist.

findings.statement: Buried masonry, cement and plaster rubble releases calcium as it weathers, pushing city soil pH up. Craul (1985) reports streetside soils in Syracuse, NY averaging about pH 8.0 (range 6.6-9.0) and Philadelphia urban soils averaging 7.6 (range 3.7-9.0), attributing the elevation to weathering building rubble together with de-icing salts. With ordinary garden plants preferring roughly pH 6.0-7.0, whole populations of urban soils sit above the comfortable band, with readings up to 9.0.
findings.detail: Craul's 1985 description of urban soils in Arboriculture & Urban Forestry reports measured soil pH of 6.6 to 9.0 in Syracuse, New York, averaging about 8.0, and 3.7 to 9.0 in Philadelphia with a mean of 7.6. He attributes the rise to calcium released by weathering building rubble made of masonry, cement and plaster, alongside de-icing salts. Ordinary garden plants want roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, so a city averaging 8.0 is a whole population of soils sitting outside the comfortable band. These are established urban soils rather than fresh building sites, so this is not a passing few months.

source.name: Craul, P.J. (1985), 'A Description of Urban Soils and Their Desired Characteristics', Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 11(11)

findings.cannot_establish: It cannot separate rubble from road salt as the cause of those particular readings. It gives no figure for how much rubble raises pH by how much, how deep the effect reaches, or how a single buried lump behaves in a garden.

findings.statement: UF/IFAS Duval County extension advice names concrete, mortar and lime-rock left in the soil after construction of a house as a contributor to higher soil pH, and the extension agent reports often seeing landscapes where soil pH changed dramatically near the street, sidewalk or home foundation.
findings.detail: The UF/IFAS Duval County Extension fact sheet, written by an extension agent, says building materials left in the soil following construction of the residence raise pH, and that he has often seen landscapes where the soil pH changed dramatically near the street, sidewalk, or home foundation. It puts the range most plants grow well in at pH 5.8 to 6.3, against a Florida average of 6.1. When pH is too high it lists iron, manganese, boron, copper and zinc as made less available, leading to deficiency. It also warns that raising pH is relatively easy while lowering an alkaline soil is hard, needing sulphur, organic matter, pine bark and acid-forming fertiliser used together over time.

source.name: UF/IFAS Extension Duval County, 'Why Soil pH Matters' (Larry Figart, Extension Agent)

findings.cannot_establish: This is practitioner experience in an extension leaflet, not measured data. No pH numbers for rubble-affected soil, no distance from the foundation, no timescale. It also does not list phosphorus among the nutrients locked out at high pH, unlike other sources.

findings.statement: UC IPM's home and landscape guidance puts the good soil pH range at 6.0 to 7.5, and says that above it iron, manganese and zinc become less available to roots. The plant shows it as "interveinal chlorosis and bleaching, pale mottling, and blotchy or marginal necrosis of new growth" — the damage lands on new growth. The nutrients are not absent from the soil; pH "affects the form and availability of nutrients and the ability of roots to absorb" them. Three corrections to the earlier version: this source names three nutrients, not four — it places phosphorus deficiency at the ACID end, under soil below pH 5.5, not above 7.5; it gives no numeric threshold for "high pH", so 7.5 is read off the stated desirable range; and it does not explain why new growth goes first (the phloem-immobility of iron and manganese is real, but needs its own citation), nor does it say that feeding those nutrients fails — its own remedies are sulfur, iron sulfate, acidifying fertilizer and pH-tolerant species.
findings.detail: UC IPM's home and landscape guidance puts the ideal soil pH at 6.0 to 7.5 and names iron, manganese, zinc and phosphorus as the nutrients that become less available to roots above it. The visible damage it describes is interveinal chlorosis and bleaching, pale mottling, and blotchy or marginal necrosis of new growth. The tell is that it strikes new growth first, because iron and manganese do not move around inside the plant, so old leaves can stay green while the tips go pale and papery. The nutrients are not absent from the soil, they are chemically locked into forms roots cannot pull in, which is why feeding the plant more of them often does nothing.

source.name: UC Statewide IPM Program (UC ANR), 'pH Problems', Home and Landscape

findings.cannot_establish: The page does not mention construction debris at all, gives no pH threshold per individual nutrient, does not say how fast symptoms appear, and does not rank which species suffer soonest. Interveinal chlorosis also has other causes, so the symptom alone is not proof of high pH.

findings.statement: Water touching fresh crushed concrete comes off at pH above 10, but in real field conditions that alkalinity falls toward neutral within about a year, far faster than lab tests predict.
findings.detail: Sanger and colleagues at UW-Madison tested recycled concrete aggregate recovered from the MnROAD highway research site. Fresh contact with water gives pH above 10 because portlandite, which is calcium hydroxide, dissolves and releases hydroxide ions. But pan lysimeters under the actual road measured leachate at pH 7.5 to 8.5 in the period just after construction, and pH 7.2 to 7.4 in samples taken eight years later. Two processes pull it down: carbon dioxide from the air converts calcium hydroxide to calcium carbonate, forming a crust on the concrete surface that blocks further dissolution, and hydroxide is also neutralised by reaction with soil minerals in the subgrade. The authors state plainly that persistently high laboratory pH is in poor agreement with the near-neutral pH measured in the field.

source.name: Sanger, Campagnola, Ritchey, Edil & Ginder-Vogel, 'Assessing the Impact of Contact Time on Leachate Chemistry from Recycled Concrete Aggregates' (Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison)

findings.cannot_establish: This is drained road base under pavement with water moving through it, not lumps of concrete and mortar sitting in slow, wet garden soil. It measures the water coming off the aggregate, not the pH of the soil around it, and says nothing about plants. Treat it as a real reason to doubt 'concrete keeps your soil alkaline forever', not as proof against it.

findings.statement: The USDA-NRCS soil quality guide for educators gives bulk densities above which root growth is restricted, and they are much lower in clay than in sand: above 1.47 g/cm3 in clays over 45% clay, versus above 1.80 in sandy loams and loams. NRCS presents this as a "general relationship," not a hard cutoff — roots are impaired rather than stopped, and growth is already affected below those numbers, at 1.39 in clay and 1.63 in a sandy loam.
findings.detail: The USDA-NRCS soil quality guide gives the full table. Bulk densities that restrict root growth: sands and loamy sands above 1.80 g/cm3, sandy loams and loams above 1.80, sandy clay loams and clay loams above 1.75, silt loams and silty clay loams above 1.65, sandy clays and silty clays above 1.58, and clays over 45% clay above 1.47. Root growth is already affected well below those numbers, at 1.63 in a sandy loam and 1.39 in clay. For scale, an ideal silt loam is about 1.33 g/cm3, which corresponds to 50% pore space. The same guide notes bulk density normally rises with depth because subsurface layers have less organic matter, less aggregation and less root penetration, which is exactly the material a stripped site leaves at the surface.

source.name: USDA-NRCS Soil Quality Kit, 'Soil Bulk Density / Moisture / Aeration — Guides for Educators'

findings.cannot_establish: These are general agricultural guide values, not species-specific, and a single number is meaningless without knowing the soil's texture. The table does not cover stony rubble fill, where bulk density is hard to measure honestly, and it does not say how long roots survive above the threshold, only that growth is restricted.

findings.statement: On sandy Florida building sites, construction activity and compaction cut water soaking into the ground by 70 to 99 percent, leaving nominally permeable ground behaving close to pavement. (In the detail, describe the 733-to-178 mm/hr result as the paper's side-by-side testing of compacted versus undisturbed areas on the same lots, not a "controlled" trial.)
findings.detail: Gregory and colleagues, in the Journal of Soil and Water Conservation (2006), measured with double-ring infiltrometers on Florida building sites. Uncompacted natural forest took water at 377 to 634 mm per hour; comparable ground after construction took 8 to 175 mm per hour. In a controlled side-by-side trial, heavy equipment dropped infiltration from 733 to 178 mm per hour while bulk density rose from 1.34 to 1.49 g/cm3. Deepest compaction sat at 20 to 30 cm below the surface, below the reach of a fork. Their own conclusion is that it mattered less how heavy the machine was than whether compaction happened at all, and that compacted pervious area effectively approaches the infiltration behavior of an impervious surface.

source.name: Gregory, Dukes, Jones & Miller (2006), 'Effect of urban soil compaction on infiltration rate', Journal of Soil and Water Conservation 61(3) — copy hosted in a US EPA docket

findings.cannot_establish: Sandy soils in north-central Florida; clays compact and drain differently and may behave worse. Double-ring infiltrometers measure water entering at the surface, so this shows water failing to get in, not where it goes afterwards. The study measures hydrology, not plant survival. Note also that the copy I read is a scanned court exhibit, not the publisher's version.

findings.statement: Colorado State University Extension states that a moist soil could reach 75% of maximum compaction the first time it is stepped on, and 90% by the fourth time. If that figure holds, most trampling compaction happens in the first few footsteps — so keeping traffic off moist ground entirely matters more than merely limiting how often it is crossed.
findings.detail: Colorado State University Extension states that a moist soil could reach 75% maximum compaction the first time it is stepped on, and 90% by the fourth time. If true, this reframes the whole problem: fencing wet ground off matters far more than limiting how often people cross it, because the fifth hundred crossing adds almost nothing to what the first one did. The same page explains the mechanism, that compaction reduces total pore space and especially the large pores, restricting air and water movement, and that low soil oxygen is a primary factor limiting plant growth. It also states that soil compaction is difficult to correct, so effort should go into preventing it.

source.name: Colorado State University Extension, 'Soil Compaction'

findings.cannot_establish: The page gives no primary citation, no soil type and no definition of 'maximum compaction', so I could not trace the figure to the original measurement. It almost certainly derives from one study on one soil at one moisture content, and should be quoted as an extension service's guidance rather than a universal constant.

findings.statement: A UK government case study documents the exact failure pattern: turf on 150 to 200 mm of topsoil over un-ripped compacted subsoil looked healthy through its first summer and collapsed the following winter.
findings.detail: The Defra Construction Code of Practice for the Sustainable Use of Soils on Construction Sites records a housing development where topsoil was stripped and stockpiled wet, coming back structureless and cloddy, while the subsoil was left in place and over-compacted by wheeled plant and stored building materials. Topsoil went down in winter 2005 at 150 to 200 mm over subsoil that had not been ripped or decompacted, and the gardens were turfed. The turf was healthy for the first summer, but by the onset of winter 2006 it began to rapidly fail and the gardens waterlogged after prolonged or heavy rain. Inspection found the topsoil structureless, waterlogged and anaerobic with virtually no root growth into it, and the subsoil relatively dry but heavily compacted, preventing drainage. Eighteen of twenty-seven gardens had to be remediated, at a cost of around ninety thousand pounds.

source.name: Defra, 'Construction Code of Practice for the Sustainable Use of Soils on Construction Sites' (UK Government)

findings.cannot_establish: One case study, on heavy loam, in a wet British winter. It does not prove every thin-topsoil lawn fails, nor that the one-to-two-year timescale is general. It describes compacted subsoil, not buried rubble specifically. The failure here also had two causes tangled together, wet-stockpiled topsoil and un-ripped subsoil, and the report does not separate them.

findings.statement: Where one soil layer meets a differently textured one, water movement pauses — and can stop — at the boundary instead of passing straight through: LSU AgCenter states that 'soil-water movement does not like a discontinuity and pauses or stops completely.' Water backs up above the interface, which can produce a perched water table and an oxygen-starved 'black layer,' and turf roots tend to stay in the layer they prefer, leaving the lawn on a shallow root mat. (The further step — that the upper layer must approach saturation before water breaks through into the layer beneath — is standard soil physics, but it is not stated on the cited LSU page and needs its own source if kept.)
findings.detail: LSU AgCenter states that soil-water movement does not like a discontinuity and pauses or stops completely, and that the upper layer has to saturate before water will move into the layer beneath. The result is a perched water table and an oxygen-starved black layer at the interface. Roots respond by staying in the layer they prefer, so they never anchor into the ground below and the whole lawn sits on a shallow mat. This is the physics behind both symptoms people actually see on new-build ground: puddles that stand for days, and water sheeting off onto the patio because the sponge above the boundary is already full.

source.name: LSU AgCenter, 'Layering in Soils'

findings.cannot_establish: Written about sports turf and sand-based rootzones, not builders' rubble. It does not quantify how thick the layers must be, how long water perches, or at what degree of texture contrast the effect begins. It is a mechanism that fits the new-build case, not a measurement of one.

findings.statement: Urban construction soil tends to be low in organic matter, and Craul gives a direct mechanism for what follows: organic matter is "a major source of energy for most soil-inhabiting organisms", so where it is lacking "the soil organism population is limited and the activity is reduced below natural soils levels". Earthworms in particular are largely absent for want of organic horizons, which further reduces aggregation and slows nutrient cycling — a loop rather than a single loss. He adds that urban soil "generally lacks the organic matter cycling and its nutrient contribution that typifies the soil of the natural ecosystem", because leaves and litter are carted off as waste instead of rotting where they fall. Two caveats the source itself supplies: Craul lists low organic matter among the causes of compaction rather than among his eight defining characteristics of urban soil, and he stresses that organic matter content varies sharply between layers of an urban profile — so "low" is a tendency measured against natural soils, not a universal. The passage carries no citation or data; it is Craul reasoning from soil-science principles in a 1985 review.
findings.detail: Craul lists low organic matter content among the defining features of urban soil, noting it both disfavours aggregation and starves the biology. His mechanism is direct: organic matter is a major source of energy for most soil-inhabiting organisms, so if it is lacking, the population is limited and activity is reduced. Earthworms are especially absent, which further reduces aggregation and slows nutrient cycling, making this a loop rather than a single loss. He also notes urban soil generally lacks the organic matter cycling and nutrient contribution that typifies a natural ecosystem, because leaves and litter are carted off as waste instead of rotting where they fall.

source.name: Craul, P.J. (1985), 'A Description of Urban Soils and Their Desired Characteristics', Arboriculture & Urban Forestry 11(11)

findings.cannot_establish: A 1985 descriptive review. It gives no measured organic matter percentages, no microbial biomass counts and no side-by-side figures against undisturbed soil. It describes urban soils in general rather than fresh construction rubble specifically. I did not find a fetchable study measuring organic matter and microbial biomass in new-build garden substrate — that is a real gap.

findings.statement: Strip the top 7.5 cm and the mycorrhizal fungi can be lost entirely — that figure comes from a greenhouse experiment with simulated erosion — and the propagules that do survive keep declining while the ground sits bare with no host plants. Heavy logging in a Malaysian forest cut the abundance and infectivity of AMF propagules by about 75 percent. The mechanism is physical: hyphae are an important source of inoculum and are highly susceptible to disturbance, so disturbing the soil lowers its infective potential rather than merely stressing what is there.
findings.detail: A review of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in restoring degraded land reports a greenhouse experiment finding that erosion of soil beyond 7.5 cm could make soil lose AMF completely. Heavy logging in a Malaysian forest cut the abundance and infectivity of AMF propagules by about 75 percent. The mechanism is physical: the fungal hyphae are themselves the main inoculum, and hyphae are fragile, so disturbance cuts the network rather than merely stressing it. Critically, the number of surviving propagules also declines with time in the absence of host plants, meaning bare compacted ground gets biologically poorer while it waits, not richer.

source.name: 'The Potential Role of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi in the Restoration of Degraded Lands' (review, PubMed Central)

findings.cannot_establish: These are greenhouse and forestry studies, not measurements on building sites. The review does not say how much AMF a rubble substrate retains, does not cover high-pH or heavily compacted substrates, and does not give a recovery timescale once plants are replanted. The 7.5 cm figure is from a single greenhouse experiment.

findings.statement: The desert comparison is sound, and it flatters the rubble: real deserts carry a living skin of cyanobacteria, fungi, lichens and mosses that does substantial biological work. Ferrenberg, Tucker and Reed of the US Geological Survey describe biological soil crusts as widespread, diverse communities of cyanobacteria, fungi, lichens and mosses living on soil surfaces, primarily in drylands, which can locally govern primary production, soil fertility, hydrology and surface energy balance — though the same paper cautions that biocrust cover across drylands remains poorly characterised. Models suggest these communities of non-vascular photoautotrophs could account for nearly 50 percent of terrestrial nitrogen fixation and 7 percent of carbon fixation globally, but the same paper says estimates vary widely, run as low as 4 percent for nitrogen, and remain highly uncertain. These organisms are not dormant curiosities: the crust cyanobacterium Microcoleus vaginatus restarts photosynthesis within an hour of being wetted, and the biocrust moss Syntrichia caninervis tolerates drying to about minus 540 megapascals against roughly minus 3 for common agricultural plants. So a desert is functioning soil with a working microbiome. That bare compacted rubble has less biology than a desert is our own inference rather than the paper's finding, but the paper points the same way: it names compaction as destroying the soil pores where cyanobacterial activity happens, and reports that a decade of repeated trampling cut biocrust chlorophyll a and microbial DNA by half.
findings.detail: Ferrenberg, Tucker and Reed of the US Geological Survey describe biological soil crusts as widespread, diverse communities of cyanobacteria, fungi, lichens and mosses living on soil surfaces, primarily in drylands, which locally govern primary production, soil fertility, hydrology and surface energy balance. Models suggest biocrusts could account for nearly 50 percent of terrestrial nitrogen fixation and 7 percent of carbon fixation globally, though the same paper says estimates vary widely, some as low as 4 percent for nitrogen, and remain highly uncertain. These organisms are not dormant curiosities: crust cyanobacteria restart photosynthesis within an hour of being wetted, and biocrust mosses tolerate drying to about minus 540 megapascals against roughly minus 3 for a common agricultural plant. So a desert is functioning soil with a working microbiome, and bare compacted rubble has less biology than a desert rather than the same amount.

source.name: Ferrenberg, Tucker & Reed (2017), 'Biological soil crusts: diminutive communities of potential global importance', Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment — USGS author manuscript via OSTI

findings.cannot_establish: The global nitrogen and carbon fixation percentages are explicitly uncertain in the paper itself, and the authors say we lack sufficient data on biocrust cover and function to confidently assess their roles across drylands. The paper says nothing about urban or construction substrates — the comparison to rubble is mine, not theirs, and no source I found measures both side by side.

findings.statement: Even a desert skin, once scraped off, takes years to centuries to regrow. A 2023 Colorado Plateau study (Jech, Havrilla & Barger, Frontiers in Microbiology) cites published estimates of 3 to 300 years for natural recovery, drawn from a review table in Weber et al. 2016. In its own plots, where biocrust was scraped down to mineral soil, chlorophyll a rose from about 2.7 to 4.3 micrograms per gram of dry soil in 1.5 years - roughly 1 microgram per year - against an undisturbed reference of 12 to 13. The sticky exopolysaccharides that glue the crust together doubled, from about 560 to 1,126 micrograms glucose per gram, against a reference of 3,000 to 3,700. Physical soil stability came back fastest, reaching high levels on the field slake scale (median 5.5 out of 6) within 1.5 years - though the study never measured stability in its undisturbed reference plots, so it cannot show full recovery, only a high score. That is the honest catch: the surface can test stable while the biology underneath is still at roughly a third of reference.
findings.detail: A Colorado Plateau study measured recovery in plots where biocrust had been completely removed, and cites natural recovery as a relatively slow process of 3 to 300 years. In the first 1.5 years after removal, chlorophyll a rose from about 2.7 to 4.3 micrograms per gram of dry soil, against an undisturbed reference of 12 to 13, an increase of roughly 1 microgram per year. The sticky exopolysaccharides that glue the crust together doubled, from about 560 to 1,126 micrograms glucose per gram, against a reference of 3,000 to 3,700. Physical soil stability came back fastest, reaching reference levels within 1.5 years, which is the honest catch: the surface can look and feel stable long before the biology underneath has actually returned.

source.name: 'The influence of disturbance scale on the natural recovery of biological soil crusts on the Colorado Plateau' (PubMed Central)

findings.cannot_establish: The direct measurements cover only 1.5 years, so the long end of the 3-to-300-year range is cited from other work rather than observed here. Plots were small, under one square metre. Nothing here transfers quantitatively to a temperate garden or to rubble — it establishes that a desert's living layer is slow to rebuild, not how fast yours would.

findings.statement: The buried-cotton idea is a real soil-science method: the cotton strip assay, standardised by Latter, P.M. & Howson, G. (1977), "The use of cotton strips to indicate cellulose decomposition in the field", Pedobiologia 17, 145-155. Strips of standard cotton cloth are buried in the soil profile, left, then recovered and pulled apart on a tensile tester — the change in tensile strength is the index of how fast cellulose is being decomposed. In one study of three French forest sites, run 1983-84 by the Institute of Terrestrial Ecology (Merlewood) and the Centre de Recherche Forestiere and published in 1988, "cotton strips were inserted in soil profiles in the winter (December-February) for 8 weeks and in summer (July) for 3 weeks" — a burial roughly two and a half times shorter in summer. Season turned out to be the single largest effect the study measured on cellulose decomposition (F ratio = 275, significant at 1%), larger than tree species or soil depth. Results are reported as a cotton rotting rate (CRR per year), not as a yes/no. For a homeowner this means burial time is not one fixed number: the same soil works far faster in summer than in winter, so the raw question "how chewed up is it after N weeks?" cannot be carried across seasons. Only the rate can be compared — which is exactly why the science converts to a rate before comparing at all.
findings.detail: The scientific version is the cotton strip assay, referenced back to Latter, P.M. & Howson, G. (1977) in Pedobiologia. Strips of standard cotton cloth are pushed down into the soil profile, left, pulled up and pulled apart on a machine to see how much strength the microbes have eaten out of them. In a 1988 forest study by the Institute of Terrestrial Ecology and the French forest research centre, the same sites needed 8 weeks of burial in winter (December-February) but only 3 weeks in summer (July) to get a readable signal. The result is expressed as a cotton rotting rate, not as a yes/no. For a homeowner this means the burial time is not a fixed number: it is whatever the season demands, and two burials in different months are not comparable.

source.name: NERC Open Research Archive (Nys & Howson 1988, ITE Symposium 24, 'Cotton strip assay: an index of decomposition in soils')

findings.cannot_establish: I could not open the 1977 Latter & Howson paper itself (paywalled), so I am relying on a 1988 chapter citing it. It does not tell you the exact fabric grade, the strip dimensions, or how to convert a homeowner's ragged pair of pants into a cotton rotting rate — there is no conversion.

findings.statement: The citizen version, 'Soil Your Undies', is 100% cotton pants buried flat 3-4 inches down for 60 days, best in late spring when the soil is moist.
findings.detail: The Pennsylvania Soil Health Coalition protocol: dig a hole big enough to lay the underwear flat, about 3-4 inches deep, photograph it, mark the spot with a flag or stick that will not move, set a 60-day reminder, then dig it up. Cotton is nearly pure cellulose, so soil life treats it as food; the more that has gone, the more feeding was happening. They say late spring is the best time and that it works best when soils are moist, because that is when the microbes are active. Polyester will survive two months in any soil, so blends ruin the test. Other bodies give different numbers for the same test (see the note on protocol drift).

source.name: Pennsylvania Soil Health Coalition

findings.cannot_establish: There is no scale on this. Nobody publishes 'X% of the cotton gone = healthy'. It gives you a photograph, not a number, and one pair in one hole tells you about one hole.

findings.statement: Farmers Weekly (New Zealand), in its DIY soil-health series, says plainly that the buried-cotton test "will not give definitive answers on soil life, and should be used for comparative purposes only." The article lists what else drives the result: soil moisture, weather, soil temperature and nutrient availability — "particularly chemical N, which gets soil bacteria hungry and excited" — plus site history such as machinery, crop types and spacing, and whether the spot is a fence line, the middle of a field, or a gateway. It advises comparing degradation across locations and recording site details for each. Two caveats: this is a how-to column by farming and science writer Sue Edmonds (August 2022), not a statement from people who run the test professionally; and the article does not prescribe burying a paired control on the same day and depth, nor does it discuss fungal-dominated soils decomposing cotton more slowly than bacterial ones. That fungal point is made elsewhere in the soil-health literature and needs its own source before it is published.
findings.detail: Farmers Weekly NZ's soil-health series quotes the caveats: biological activity is also driven by soil moisture, weather, soil temperature and nutrient availability — particularly chemical nitrogen, which makes bacteria hungry. Site history matters too: machinery, crop type, fence line versus middle of field versus gateway. Their conclusion is that results will not give definitive answers on soil life and should be used for comparative purposes only. They also flag a genuine trap: fungal-dominated soils decompose cotton more slowly than bacterial ones, and fungal dominance is usually a good sign, so slow rot can mean good soil. The practical fix is to always bury two pairs — one in the ground you are judging, one in a patch you already trust — on the same day, same depth.

source.name: Farmers Weekly (New Zealand), DIY soil health series

findings.cannot_establish: This is farming trade press summarising agronomists, not a peer-reviewed limitation study. The fungal-slow-decomposer point is plausible and widely repeated but I did not find a controlled experiment proving that healthy fungal soils reliably rot cotton slower than healthy bacterial ones.

findings.statement: The standard worm spit is a 20 x 20 x 20 cm block of soil, hand-sorted for five minutes, repeated at ten spots across the ground in a W shape. This is the #60minworms protocol used in an England-wide on-farm survey — 126 fields, over 1,300 hectares of farmland, in spring 2018. Ten pits per field in a W pattern; five minutes of hand sorting each, extended to ten minutes if the soil is too wet or compacted; adult worms sorted into three life-styles — epigeic (small red worms), endogeic (pale or green worms), anecic (heavily pigmented, large worms). The pass/fail rule is about which kinds are present, not raw numbers: a field counted as sub-optimal if at least one of the three groups turned up in one pit or fewer out of the ten (≤10% presence), and 42% of fields failed that test. The authors also measured their own blindness: re-sorting the same soil for another five minutes found 1.6 ± 0.17 more worms per pit — 91% of them juveniles, which the scoring does not count — working out to about 40 worms per square metre missed.
findings.detail: This is the #60minworms protocol used in an England-wide on-farm survey (over 1,300 pits). Ten pits per field in a W pattern; five minutes of hand sorting each, extended to ten minutes if the soil is too wet or compacted; adults sorted into three life-styles — epigeic (small red surface worms), endogeic (pale or green soil worms), anecic (big, heavily pigmented, deep burrowers). The pass/fail rule is about which kinds are present, not raw numbers: a field scoring 10% or less presence for at least one ecological group counted as sub-optimal, and 42% of fields failed on that test. The authors also measured their own blindness: re-sorting the same soil for another five minutes found 1.6 more worms per pit on average, about 40 worms per square metre missed.

source.name: PLOS ONE / PMC — 'Soil health pilot study in England: outcomes from an on-farm earthworm survey' (Stroud 2019)

findings.cannot_establish: This was designed for farm fields, not gardens; ten pits in a small garden may be more digging than the ground can stand. It also shows the count is an undercount by design — five minutes of hand sorting always misses worms.

findings.statement: As a rough number: nine or more worms per spade-sized pit (a 20x20x20 cm block) is good, three or fewer is bad — though AHDB's method builds that picture from about ten pits across a field, not from one hole.
findings.detail: That is the benchmark AHDB (the UK levy board) published with its Soil Health Scorecard, which grades each indicator green (monitor), amber (review) or red (investigate). Nine or more earthworms in cropped land is good; three or fewer is bad. Treat these as coarse traffic lights, not precision. AHDB is explicit that the benchmarks apply to mineral topsoils under crops and lowland grassland, and not to upland grass, semi-natural systems or peaty and organic soils. For a garden, the honest use is: zero or one or two worms across several pits, in damp spring soil, is a red flag worth acting on; nine-plus is a reassurance, not a certificate.

source.name: AHDB (Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board), UK

findings.cannot_establish: I could not open the underlying benchmark tables, so I cannot give you the middle band, per-soil-type variation, or a separate grassland figure. There is no published benchmark at all for a domestic garden or a new-build plot.

findings.statement: Count worms in early spring, or in autumn after the soil has wetted up — and ideally when the soil has already been wet for a few days. AHDB calls these the best conditions rather than a strict rule: it says the soil "should have been wet for a few days prior to sampling" and that you should avoid sampling when the soil is very dry.
findings.detail: AHDB's 'How to count earthworms' sheet: dig the 20 x 20 x 20 cm pit onto a mat, sort by hand, separate adults (which have a clear saddle, the reproductive ring) from juveniles, identify the adults, and return the juveniles to the pit. It says to sample early in the spring or after the soil has wetted up in the autumn, that the soil should have been wet for a few days prior to sampling, and to avoid very dry soil. Washington State University's Master Gardener DIY sheet gives the same idea in kitchen terms for a garden: wait until the soil is at least 55°F and damp but not sopping wet, dig one cubic foot, sort it on cardboard, and ten worms is a pass.

source.name: AHDB, 'How to count earthworms'

findings.cannot_establish: It gives no temperature threshold and no numeric thresholds at all — it points you at the scorecard for those. The WSU cubic-foot/ten-worms rule (https://s3.wp.wsu.edu/uploads/sites/2076/2024/07/C221-DIY-Soil-Testing.pdf, also fetched) is a gardener heuristic, not a validated benchmark.

findings.statement: A worm count taken in dry or hot soil can badly underread. Penn State Extension notes that when soils dry out earthworms may move to deeper layers, die, or enter a dormant state called diapause — in which they are "tied up in a knot in a little hole that is lined with a slimy substance to avoid moisture loss" — and that "earthworm populations in Pennsylvania are low in the summer" because of dry conditions. Deep-burrowing (anecic) species live in permanent vertical burrows up to 5 or 6 feet deep, well below spade depth. Note that the summer low is partly worms hiding and partly worms actually dying, so a poor July count is genuinely ambiguous rather than simply wrong. Penn State's page offers no sampling guidance; for that, other extension services (e.g. AHDB) recommend counting in mid-March to April or in October, on soil that has been moist for several days, and avoiding summer or very dry ground. Practical upshot: a low count in baked August soil tells you little; a low count in damp spring soil is worth taking seriously.
findings.detail: Penn State Extension describes diapause: earthworms in diapause are tied up in a knot in a little hole lined with a slimy substance to avoid moisture loss. It also states plainly that earthworm populations in Pennsylvania are low in the summer. And the deep-burrowing anecic worms live in permanent vertical burrows that can be five or six feet deep — far below any spade. So a July count in baked ground measures the weather, not the soil. This is the single most important practical warning for a homeowner: a zero in August is meaningless; a zero in damp April soil is real information.

source.name: Penn State Extension, 'Earthworms'

findings.cannot_establish: It gives no counting protocol and no threshold, and its one density figure (70 per square foot in one grassland study) is a single study, not a norm. It does not tell you how long after rain the worms come back up.

findings.statement: The Earthworm Society of Britain's sampling protocol offers a mustard solution as an alternative to digging: mix 25 ml of mustard powder into 0.75 litre of tap water and shake well, pour it over the ground, then keep checking that patch and the area around it for ten minutes to see if any earthworms emerge. Any adults that appear can be taken and preserved for identification. The Society's own stated reason for the method is access, not depth — "on some sites it may not be possible to get permission to dig" — and it is offered instead of digging rather than as an extra step alongside it. Their standard hand-sorted pit for the National Earthworm Recording Scheme is 25 cm by 25 cm to a depth of 10 cm, five pits per site: wider and shallower than the AHDB farm pit's 20 cm cube. That mustard expellants bring up deep-burrowing anecic worms a shallow pit misses, and that the active irritant is allyl isothiocyanate — the compound that makes mustard hot — is well supported in the soil-biology literature (Zaborski 2003, Applied Soil Ecology), but appears nowhere on the ESB page. Cite that separately or drop it.
findings.detail: The Earthworm Society of Britain's sampling protocol: mix 25 ml of mustard powder into 0.75 litre of tap water and shake well, pour it over the area, then keep checking that patch and the ground around it for ten minutes for worms coming up. Any adults that surface can be collected and identified. Their standard hand-sorted pit for the National Earthworm Recording Scheme is 25 cm by 25 cm to a depth of 10 cm — shallower and wider than the AHDB farm pit, which is why the mustard step matters: the big anecic worms live below it. The mustard is a vermifuge; the active irritant is allyl isothiocyanate, the same compound that makes mustard hot.

source.name: Earthworm Society of Britain, sampling protocol (National Earthworm Recording Scheme)

findings.cannot_establish: The page states no area for that 0.75 litre, no season, no thresholds, and no limitations. Research literature reports concentrations from roughly 10 to 75 g of powder per litre, so 'mustard water' is not one standardised thing, and mustard strength varies by jar and by use-by date. It cannot reach worms that are already dormant deep down.

findings.statement: The jar test reads a soil's skeleton — sand, silt and clay — in about 48 hours, and says nothing about whether that soil is alive. Clemson's method: fill a straight-sided jar one third with soil, top up with water, shake to a slurry, then mark sand at one minute, silt at two hours, clay at 48 hours, and read the class off a soil texture triangle. Other extension versions (e.g. Montana State, Oregon State — not the cited Clemson page) add a dispersant such as a heaped tablespoon of Calgon per quart jar for a cleaner clay separation, since undispersed clay flocculates and settles early, making soil read sandier than it is; those versions also note that anything left floating is organic matter.
findings.detail: Clemson's method: fill a straight-sided jar one third with soil, top up with clean water leaving an air gap, cap it and shake until it is a uniform slurry. Set it level. At one minute, mark the sand layer. At two hours, mark the silt. At 48 hours, mark the clay. Measure each band and the total, work out three percentages, and read the class off a soil texture triangle. Organic matter floats or stays in suspension and colours the water. Extension versions that add a dispersant (about a heaped tablespoon of Calgon or similar per quart jar) get a cleaner clay separation, because without it clay flocculates and settles early, which makes the soil read sandier than it is.

source.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension, Home & Garden Information Center

findings.cannot_establish: The Clemson sheet lists no limitations and no dispersant. The jar test cannot detect life, structure, compaction or contamination, and it is a measurement of only the fine earth — anything over 2 mm has to be picked out first, which is exactly where rubble hides.

findings.statement: There is a written specification for what counts as topsoil rather than fill — BS 3882:2015, the British Standard for topsoil that is moved or traded — and a striking share of it is limits on what must NOT be in there (visible contaminants, plastics, sharps, phytotoxic metals), alongside positive requirements for texture, organic matter, pH and nutrients.
findings.detail: BS 3882:2015 is the British Standard for topsoil that is moved or traded. As summarised by an accredited soil-analysis lab: for multipurpose topsoil, visible contaminants over 2 mm must be under 0.5% by mass, of which plastics under 0.25%, and sharps must be zero in 1 kg of air-dried soil. Organic matter by loss on ignition must be 3-20% for soils with 5-20% clay, or 5-20% for 20-35% clay. The standard is explicitly not intended for grading topsoil in situ, so it is not a legal test of your garden — but it is the number a homeowner can point at. In a jar test, brick dust, mortar and crushed concrete show up as an angular, pale, gritty bottom layer that will not ribbon, plus fizzing when you drop vinegar on it (mortar and concrete are full of carbonate), and a pH pushed up towards 8.

source.name: Cawood Scientific / NRM Laboratories technical advice sheet on BS3882:2015

findings.cannot_establish: This is a testing laboratory's summary of a paywalled British Standard — the lab sells the analysis, so it profits from people caring about this. I could not read BS 3882:2015 itself. The description of how rubble looks in a jar is my own inference from the carbonate and particle-size evidence below, not a quoted finding; no source I fetched describes a rubble jar directly.

findings.statement: Drive a ring into the ground, pour in exactly one inch of water, and time it. In the USDA-NRCS guide's own worked example (same silty clay loam field), the inch vanished in one minute on uncompacted soil off the wheel track, while on the compacted wheel track the same inch took three hours.
findings.detail: USDA-NRCS Soil Quality Kit method: clear the surface, drive a 3-inch-diameter ring to a depth of 3 inches, firm the soil inside the rim, line the ring with plastic wrap draped over the side, pour in 107 ml (that is one inch of water for that ring), gently pull the wrap away and start the clock. Stop when the surface is 'glistening'. Repeat with a second inch — that second one is the steady-state rate and the one worth comparing. The guide's own worked example, same silty clay loam field: wheel track, first inch 180 minutes (0.33 in/hr); non-wheel track, first inch 1 minute, second inch 120 minutes (0.5 in/hr). Steady rates by texture: sands over 0.8 in/hr, sandy and silty soils 0.4-0.8, loams 0.2-0.4, clayey soils 0.04-0.2, sodic clayey soils under 0.04. Roughly 0.04 in/hr is 1 mm/hr and 0.8 in/hr is 20 mm/hr.

source.name: USDA-NRCS Soil Quality Kit 'Guides for Educators: Soil Infiltration' (hosted by Envirothon PA)

findings.cannot_establish: The guide says a single ring measurement is only an estimate and several should be run, and warns not to test unusually dry soil. It gives no poor/fair/good grading — only a comparison against texture. It cannot tell you whether a slow reading is a surface crust, a buried slab, or just clay.

findings.statement: A fast infiltration reading is not proof of life. The NRCS guide states that some clayey soils develop shrinkage cracks as they dry, and that "the cracks are direct conduits for water entering the soil, causing clayey soils to have high infiltration rates under dry conditions." Its own table puts sands — an inherent texture the guide says cannot be changed — at the top, above 0.8 in/hr steady-state. So a quick first inch is consistent with living crumb structure and equally consistent with dry cracked clay or bare sand. (Rubble and hardcore drink fast too, but that is general physics; this guide does not discuss them.) The reverse reading is not clean either: the guide names surface crusting, compaction and restrictive layers as things that slow infiltration, but it also says clayey soils without cracks simply have slow rates by texture alone — so a slow, ponding result is a reason to look closer, not proof of damage. What biology does here is the slow end of the range: organic matter binds particles into stable aggregates, and soil biota "create continuous pores linking surface soil layers to subsurface soil layers." Follow the guide's own protocol: do not test when the surface soil is unusually dry — wet it and let it soak, or test after rain or irrigation — and always run a second inch, since the table's values are only meant to be compared against that second inch.
findings.detail: The same NRCS guide states that some clayey soils develop shrinkage cracks as they dry, that the cracks are direct conduits for water entering the soil, and that this causes clayey soils to have high infiltration rates under dry conditions. Sands are the fastest texture in its own table (over 0.8 in/hr) with no biology required. Meanwhile the guide's account of what biology does is about the slow end: organic matter binds particles into stable aggregates, and soil biota create continuous pores linking surface layers to subsurface layers. So the test's honest reading is one-directional. A slow, ponding, sealed result is strong evidence something is wrong — crusting, compaction, a restrictive layer. A fast result is consistent with living crumb structure, and equally consistent with sand, cracks or hardcore. Test after rain or irrigation, never on baked ground, and always run a second inch.

source.name: USDA-NRCS Soil Quality Kit 'Guides for Educators: Soil Infiltration' (hosted by Envirothon PA)

findings.cannot_establish: The guide never says 'fast infiltration can mean dead soil' — that is my reading of its own texture table plus its cracking caveat. I found no study measuring infiltration through builders' rubble under a thin turf layer, so the rubble half of this is inference, not evidence.

findings.statement: The vinegar fizz is a real field test, but it measures chalk and lime in the soil, not pH — and you can even make it semi-quantitative by counting drops.
findings.detail: University of Florida IFAS published a drop-count version: one full cap of soil (about 0.8 tsp), add supermarket white vinegar at 5% acidity in ten-drop increments while stirring, and stop when vigorous bubbles go weak and a one-minute wait gives almost nothing. Under 10 drops means under 2% carbonate; 50-100 drops means 5-10%. They report a correlation of R² = 0.94 against a laboratory calcimeter. The professional field version uses 1 M hydrochloric acid and five named classes — noneffervescent (no bubbles detected), very slightly (few bubbles seen), slightly (bubbles readily seen), strongly (bubbles form low foam), violently (thick foam forms quickly) — and the USDA note says outright that effervescence is not a precise indicator but a relative index of the amount of carbonates. For a homeowner on a new-build plot this is genuinely useful: a strong fizz on ground that should be neutral loam is a mortar-and-concrete signature.

source.name: University of Florida IFAS Extension, publication HS1262

findings.cannot_establish: Carbonate content is not pH. A soil can be acidic and still contain some carbonate grains, and a soil can be strongly alkaline from sodium with no fizz at all. No fizz tells you almost nothing. The bicarbonate-of-soda half of the kitchen test has no equivalent scientific version I could find — a bicarbonate solution is only weakly alkaline, so it is a poor acid detector.

findings.statement: Kitchen pH tests tell you a direction, not a number: WSU Extension's DIY sheet says its vinegar-and-baking-soda test can tell you "toward which end of the soil pH scale your soil is leaning, but for an exact measurement, you will need to send a soil sample out to a lab." In one small SDSU Extension comparison — four cheap kits, five soils, a single sample each — the kits "generally estimated soil pH within a unit of what was measured at the lab," though the worst was off by up to 1.5 units. Their nutrient readings were far less reliable: on three soils where lab phosphorus came back high, the Rapitest kit still recommended adding phosphorus fertiliser. One pH unit is a tenfold difference in acidity, so "within a unit" is not good enough to decide on lime — only the lab tells you what to actually add.
findings.detail: Washington State University Extension's DIY sheet gives the kitchen method — one teaspoon of soil in each of two pots, half a cup of vinegar in one (fizz means alkaline), soil made muddy with distilled water plus baking soda in the other (fizz means acidic) — and then says flatly that home tests can tell you which end of the scale your soil is leaning towards, but for an exact measurement you need to send a sample to a lab. South Dakota State University Extension tested cheap consumer kits against lab results and found they generally estimated soil pH within a unit of what the lab measured, but were much worse on nutrients: on three soils where lab phosphorus was high, one popular kit still recommended adding phosphorus fertiliser. One pH unit is a tenfold difference in acidity, so 'within a unit' is not good enough to decide on lime.

source.name: South Dakota State University Extension

findings.cannot_establish: SDSU tested a handful of kits on a handful of soils, not electronic probe meters, which are widely reported to drift badly in soil. Neither source gives an error figure for the vinegar/bicarbonate method itself — nobody appears to have measured how often it gets the direction right.

findings.statement: Drop an air-dried lump of soil into water, watch it for five minutes, then lift it clear and lower it again five times over. Losing half its structure within the first five seconds is the lowest stability class on the USDA-NRCS scale; 75-100% of it still on the mesh after the five dips is the highest. The guide calls this a qualitative indicator of soil biological activity — its own line is that "binding of soil particles must constantly be renewed by biological processes" — but stability also tracks clay, texture and sodicity, so it reads as evidence about biological glue only when you compare like soil against like, which is exactly what the homeowner version does: the ground in question beside ground you trust, same soil type.
findings.detail: The USDA-NRCS slake test is a proper graded scale, not just a demonstration. Collect 16 air-dry surface fragments (about 1 cm for tilled soil), put them on mesh baskets, lower into water 2 cm deep at roughly soil temperature, and watch for five minutes. Then raise the basket clear and lower it again, one second up and one second down, five times total. Classes: 1 = half the structure lost within 5 seconds; 2 = half lost between 5 and 30 seconds; 3 = half lost between 30 and 300 seconds, or under 10% left after 5 dips; 4 = 10-25% left; 5 = 25-75% left; 6 = 75-100% left. Class 0 means the soil was too unstable to even sample. The guide's own framing is the key sentence for this whole subject: soil stability is a qualitative indicator of biological activity, and the binding of soil particles must constantly be renewed by biological processes. The homeowner version (WSU) needs two 32 oz jars and two squares of quarter-inch mesh: compare a lump from the ground in question against a lump from ground you trust.

source.name: USDA-NRCS Soil Quality Test Kit Guide, ch. 9 'Slake Test' (hosted by UC Davis SAREP)

findings.cannot_establish: The guide calls the test qualitative and requires air-dry fragments — testing a wet clod gives a false pass. High clay or a sodium problem changes slaking for reasons that have nothing to do with biology, and a cemented lump of hardcore will also 'pass' by not falling apart. It cannot tell a living crumb from a dead clod that happens to be hard.

findings.statement:
Every one of these cheap tests reads absence more readily than presence, and two of the six say nothing about life in either direction.

Tests that read no life at all: the jar test (sand/silt/clay only) and the vinegar/bicarbonate test (carbonate and rough pH).

Tests that indicate absence strongly and presence weakly: infiltration — a sealed, ponding result is real evidence of trouble, but a fast result is equally explained by sand, dry cracks or rubble (NRCS's own guide notes cracks are direct conduits causing high rates in dry clay) — and the slake test, where instant collapse is strong evidence the biological glue is gone, though sodium or plain low organic matter can disperse a lump too, and a lump that holds could be clay or cement.
